To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
melatonin is involved in the pathogenesis of experimental autoimmune arthritis in mice.
melatonin stimulates the immune system, and this stimulation can cause exacerbation of collagen‐inducetd arthritis in mice.

(i) pinealectomy ameliorated the severity of the collagen II‐inducible arthritis in mice, (ii) pinealectomies reduced the serum levels of melatonin, (iii) pinealectomes also reduced the serum levels anti‐collagen antibodies, and (iv) pinealectomed mice were less sensitive than the controls to the induction of arthritis by immunization with type II collagen.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of melatonin in autoimmune diseases.
the effects of melatonergic agents on the course of autoimmune arthritis.
the role of melatonin in the regulation of the immune system, and we are currently investigating the mechanisms involved in melatonin‐induced stimulation of the immune response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the melatonin system is involved in regulation of immune responses, which is of interest in view of the fact that the pineal gland is not only a photoreceptive organ, but also has a neuroendocrine and immune function.
melatonin stimulates the immune system and that this stimulation can cause exacerbation of the immune‐induced autoimmune disease collagen II arthritis.
melatonin is not a factor in the development of autoimmune diseases, but it can be an aggravating factor in the course of such diseases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pineal gland is an important modulatory organ of the immune system.
melatonin has dual effects on the immune system, and the net result is determined by the balance between the stimulating and the suppressing effects of melatonin.
pinealectomy and exposure to light ameliorate collagen‐induced autoimmune arthritis in mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pineal gland‐derived melatonin plays an important role in the development of autoimmune arthritis in mice.
melatonin is not a friend of the immune system, but rather an enemy, which is able to stimulate the autoimmune response.
the pineal gland is an important organ for the control of autoimmune arthritis, and melatonin may be a target for therapeutic interventions.
